item.title: Quantitative Hedge Fund Withdraws From Commercial Real Estate After Failed Fundraise
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Two Sigma closed its real estate unit to new capital and cut senior staff after raising less than half its $2 billion target amid industry-wide fundraising challenges.

The post Quantitative Hedge Fund Withdraws From Commercial Real Estate After Failed Fundraise appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Two Sigma Investments shut down new investment activity at its real estate unit and cut senior staff, including partner and chief investment officer Rich Gomel, two years after opening the business to outside investors. The quantitative hedge fund firm had targeted roughly $2 billion for the venture but raised less than half that amount. The firm will maintain a skeleton crew to manage existing properties but is no longer fundraising or deploying capital.

Two Sigma launched its real estate unit in 2019 with internal capital and opened it to outside investors in 2024 through its Real Estate Opportunity Fund, which concentrated on housing and industrial properties. The firm applied its quantitative data expertise to predict supply and demand patterns in commercial real estate markets. The Teacher Retirement System of Texas committed approximately $135 million across the main fund and a co-investment vehicle. Former Blackstone Vice Chairman Tom Hill, who served as chief executive of the business, departed in 2025.

Private real estate fundraising totaled just over $30 billion in the third quarter, the lowest quarterly figure since early 2013, according to PEI Group data. Higher interest rates have compressed property values and forced firms to extend hold periods, making capital commitments scarce across the sector. Two Sigma manages about $85 billion firmwide and has faced internal upheaval as its two founders remain locked in a prolonged dispute.

Bloomberg
Two Sigma Halts Real Estate Unit Fundraising and Cuts Staff

item.title: Owners Are Drowning in Jobsite Data and Still Guessing at the Schedule
item.dc:creator: Chaitanya Naredla Krishna
item.description:
Construction reality capture creates vast jobsite data, but owners need schedule-linked insights to make faster, defensible project decisions.

The post Owners Are Drowning in Jobsite Data and Still Guessing at the Schedule appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Owners are spending more on jobsite documentation than at any point in this industry’s history, and most of them still cannot tell you with confidence whether a subcontractor is on schedule. In most of the owner project reviews I am involved in, somebody always asks how a scope of work is tracking. Then there is always a short pause. Then two or three people give slightly different answers, none of them dishonest, and the meeting moves to the next item because nobody in the room has a better instrument than the people in the room.

What is strange about that pause is how well documented the project usually is. Weekly 360-degree walks, drone flights a couple of times a month, laser scans at the milestones, and somewhere a folder holding forty thousand photographs. Every square foot of that building has been recorded, and still, when the question gets asked out loud, the honest answer is a range.

The distance between capturing what is happening on a site and understanding it well enough, and fast enough, to do something about it is not a data problem in the way our industry usually means that phrase. There is plenty of data. What is missing is the step between the data and the decision, and that step is still being performed by a person with a spreadsheet on a Sunday night.

The underlying mistake is one a lot of us made in the first wave of reality capture. We treated the record as the outcome. If the site was fully documented, we assumed the visibility problem was handled. It is not. Forty thousand photographs are an archive, and an archive only answers questions you already knew to ask. It will not tell you, for instance, that drywall on three floors has been quietly running four days behind the curve your schedule assumed since the second week of August. That surfaces later, usually in a conversation about liquidated damages.

Autodesk and FMI surveyed more than 3,900 construction professionals for their 2021 report, Harnessing the Data Advantage in Construction, and only 12 percent said they always use project data when making decisions. The same study pinned 14 percent of all rework in 2020 on bad data, which it valued at close to 89 billion dollars. An earlier FMI study put the share of captured data that goes entirely unused at 95.5 percent. Those studies are five and eight years old. Everything about capture has improved since then, and I am not convinced the decision layer has moved much at all.

Capture hardware got cheap enough that it stopped being a decision and became a default, so the volume coming off every site keeps multiplying whether or not anyone has a plan for it. At the other end, the large project management platforms have started buying reality capture companies outright, at prices that make very little sense if the cameras are the point. They are not paying for the cameras. They are paying for the layer that sits above the imagery and turns it into an answer, because that is where the defensible position is. Capture is becoming a commodity input, roughly the way GPS did, and the margin moved up a level while most owners were still procuring capture as a line item.

The owner holds the real exposure on a capital project. You sign the guarantee, you carry the cost of capital, you answer to the lender, and you absorb whatever a late certificate of occupancy does to a lease-up schedule. Then you manage that exposure using the least rigorous instrument anywhere on the job, which is a narrative report, assembled by hand, describing conditions already a week old, written by the party whose performance it describes. I am not suggesting bad faith here. Most of the people writing those reports are doing careful work under real time pressure. But no lender would accept a borrower’s own summary of the collateral and call it diligence. It is worth asking why we accept the equivalent on a project.

Most of this is fixable in the contract rather than the budget. The most immediately actionable changes are specification changes, and they are worth the argument. The first is specifying what capture has to produce rather than just how often it happens. Most owner agreements set a documentation cadence and stop there, but cadence without a latency requirement only fills the archive faster. Agreeing on specific metrics, in a specific format, within a defined window after each capture is the step most contracts skip.

It is also important to determine definitions before anyone actually pours concrete. Things like: what percent complete does a job need to be before it is considered complete” What observable conditions constitute completion for each major milestone? These answers then need to be tied back to a schedule activity ID. Nearly every pay application dispute traces back to two parties who never agreed on a definition and then tried to negotiate one under time pressure with money already in dispute. Putting time-stamped visual evidence on the pay application as a standard exhibit gets read as adversarial, but most draw disputes are not about bad faith.

Owners running multiple active projects should also standardize across the portfolio, because six projects with six reporting formats and six working definitions of complete produce no real ability to compare risk until one job fails loudly enough to get attention. Best practice is also to specify in writing that the capture record belongs to the owner and survives a change of contractor.

If you take one thing from this, change the number you manage to. Stop reporting on how much of the site was captured last month, and start tracking how many days pass between something happening physically on site and someone with authority acting on it. That number might be unflattering the first time you measure it, which is exactly why it is useful.

There is real movement toward agentic systems that do not simply report but flag, forecast, and initiate, and I expect that to arrive faster than most capital programs are prepared for. But an agent pointed at an unstructured pile of photographs will produce confident, well-formatted guesses, and a confident guess inside a draw approval workflow is worse than no automation at all. Whatever autonomy turns out to be useful will need a structured, schedule-linked, consistently defined record underneath it. The owners sorting out their definitions and their cadence this year are doing the unglamorous work that makes the rest of it possible. The next competitive layer in this business is not going to be more cameras. It is going to be how long it takes for what a building knows about itself to reach the people who are financially responsible for it.

The post Owners Are Drowning in Jobsite Data and Still Guessing at the Schedule appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Class B Office Visitation Settles Into New Normal at 72% of Pre-Pandemic Levels
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Class B office visitation in New York City stabilizes at 72% of pre-pandemic levels, with sharp divergence between well-positioned buildings and struggling assets.

The post Class B Office Visitation Settles Into New Normal at 72% of Pre-Pandemic Levels appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Class B office buildings across Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens reached 72% of pre-pandemic visitation levels in August 2026 and have held that range for two years, according to a Real Estate Board of New York analysis of 200 properties. Midtown performed best among submarkets at 89% of pre-pandemic activity, while Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn/Queens hovered around 70%. Midtown South lagged but showed recent improvement. Twenty percent of properties studied now exceed their pre-pandemic visitation rates.

The city’s Class B inventory totals more than 235 million square feet across 1,500 buildings, housing small and mid-sized businesses, nonprofits, creative firms, and technology startups. Properties with experienced ownership, strong transit access, and diversified tenant rosters recovered faster than buildings hit by major tenant losses or coworking contractions. Forty-one percent of analyzed properties reached at least 80% of pre-pandemic visitation. REBNY executive vice president Basha Gerhards said policy must account for the wide performance gap between buildings that can compete for tenants and those facing structural challenges.

Class A availability has tightened and companies have increased in-office requirements, but those shifts have not yet pushed significant tenant migration into Class B space. Local Law 97 carbon emission limits add new investment costs that will shape decisions about repositioning versus conversion. Tax incentives including REAP and RACE support tenant recruitment at viable properties, while office-to-residential conversion programs offer an exit for buildings with prolonged vacancy.

The divergence between stabilized and struggling Class B assets will determine how this segment contributes to the city’s office recovery. Buildings with steady demand and modernization capacity face a different outlook than properties with structural obsolescence or major vacancy. Owners now must evaluate whether their buildings can still compete for tenants or whether conversion offers a better long-term path.

NYREJ
New REBNY Analysis Finds NYC Class B Office Visitation Stabilizing After Years of Post-Pandemic Recovery

item.title: Local Investors Step Into D.C. Office Bargains as Institutions Retreat
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Smaller investors are acquiring D.C. offices at steep discounts as institutional owners exit the market, planning renovations to capture tenant demand.

The post Local Investors Step Into D.C. Office Bargains as Institutions Retreat appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Smaller investors are acquiring D.C. office buildings at steep discounts as institutional owners offload properties at losses. John Mason’s Garfield Investments and Broad Creek Capital bought 1667 K Street NW for $26.2 million in July, 59% below its assessed value of $64.1 million. Taicoon Property Partners acquired 1400 K Street NW for $35.5 million, less than half its assessed value. FarmViewVentures bought 1250 Connecticut Avenue NW at foreclosure for $16 million, down from a $50 million valuation.

BGRE, formerly Brookfield Properties, has trimmed its D.C. portfolio from 31 buildings totaling 8 million square feet in 2012 to 11 buildings at roughly 3 million square feet today. The company faces a $377 million loan maturity on six properties that entered special servicing in August. James Campbell Co. sold four offices across the region in recent months, pivoting from office to industrial. Tishman Speyer sold 900 19th Street NW for about $30 million, less than half its assessed value.

Buyers plan substantial renovations to compete for tenants priced out of trophy space. Garfield and Broad Creek will invest $10 million at 1667 K Street, while FarmViewVentures plans $15 million at 1250 Connecticut. Class A office space in D.C. absorbed 218,400 square feet in the third quarter, the highest quarterly leasing activity since late 2024, according to CBRE. Sheppard law firm signed a 107,227-square-foot pre-lease at 2033 K Street NW, where In-Rel Properties plans a redevelopment of a building acquired for $20.5 million.

Institutional investors are redirecting capital to infrastructure and data centers as office returns remain uncertain. Brookfield Asset Management holds $262 billion in infrastructure assets and owns stakes in multiple data center platforms. Philadelphia’s Post Brothers, historically focused on office-to-residential conversions, now plans to develop new Class A office to capture tenant demand. Local investors say reduced acquisition costs allow them to fund renovations and achieve returns unavailable to sellers carrying legacy debt.

Why Smaller Real Estate Investors Are Having a Moment in the DC Area

item.title: 3D Construction Printing Company Lands $1.4 Billion Valuation With Dual-Use Strategy
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Icon Technology raises $200 million at a $1.4 billion valuation, scaling 3D construction printers for housing, military, and lunar projects.

The post 3D Construction Printing Company Lands $1.4 Billion Valuation With Dual-Use Strategy appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Icon Technology Inc. closed a $200 million series D funding round on October 13, co-led by Baillie Gifford and BlackRock-managed funds. The round values the Austin-based 3D construction printing company at $1.4 billion. Other investors included Capital Factory, Moonshots Capital, Overmatch, The Syndicate, CAZ Investments, Moderne Ventures, Norwest, and Tiger Global. Co-founder and CEO Jason Ballard said the valuation represents a healthy increase from the prior round and carries weight given it was set by two of the world’s largest investment firms.

Icon operates three business units: Build, which designs and constructs housing; Prime, which focuses on government and military contracts; and Tech, which handles software and R&D. All three units are profitable, and Ballard said the company is on track to roughly quadruple revenue this year. Icon has built about 270 structures to date, a third of which were for social housing projects including Community First! Village in Austin. The company recently launched Titan, a multi-story robotic construction system that sells for nearly $900,000 and requires a $5,000 reservation deposit. Ballard said reservations are running at ten times the company’s production capacity for next year.

Icon currently manufactures two to three Titan printers per month from its Austin factory and expects to outgrow that capacity by 2028. The company employs about 300 people and plans to grow to over 1,000 within a few years, with the Austin footprint expected to more than double in two years. Icon is also advancing toward potential NASA contracts for lunar construction through its Artemis program work, developing printers that could use moon regolith and ice to build structures. The company has passed NASA thermal vacuum chamber tests and conducted a Blue Origin space flight test using actual moon dust.

Ballard said development work for lunar construction has informed Icon’s terrestrial products, with the Titan printer sharing the same form factor as the lunar Olympus printer and using software originally developed for moon applications. Icon remains committed to social housing projects despite investor pressure, with Ballard describing a Robin Hood strategy where high-end, scale, and government work mature the technology for application to those most in need of dignified housing. The company expects revenue to at least double again next year across both Build and Prime business units.

Austin Business Journal
Icon Raises $200M to Build More 3D Printing Robots

The post 3D Construction Printing Company Lands $1.4 Billion Valuation With Dual-Use Strategy appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Private Lenders Fuel Investor Rush Into Distressed Rust Belt Housing
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Debt-service coverage ratio loans bypass traditional underwriting to fund investor acquisition and renovation of distressed single-family homes in Rust Belt cities.

The post Private Lenders Fuel Investor Rush Into Distressed Rust Belt Housing appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Debt-service coverage ratio loans have opened previously redlined neighborhoods to investor capital by approving borrowers based on property value and projected rental income rather than personal creditworthiness. The product, which emerged in the mid-2010s from private lenders, has directed money into East Cleveland, Indianapolis, Baltimore, Detroit, and Memphis — cities where traditional mortgage underwriting long discouraged investment. Private lenders evaluate the asset and its cash flow potential, bypassing the borrower risk models that once kept institutional capital out of distressed markets.

The loans allow investors to acquire, renovate, and lease vacant or deteriorating single-family homes in neighborhoods that federal guidance once flagged as too risky for conventional lending. Speed and flexible underwriting have made the product popular among small and mid-size investors targeting low-cost inventory as housing prices climb in primary markets. The model has also drawn scrutiny for fraud susceptibility, though the article does not detail specific cases or enforcement actions.

Debt-service coverage ratio lending represents a shift in how capital reaches tertiary housing markets. Traditional mortgage products require borrower income verification and credit checks; the new loans treat single-family rentals as income-producing assets comparable to small multifamily properties. The financing has enabled a wave of buy-renovate-rent activity in markets where property values alone would not support conventional mortgage approval, effectively creating liquidity in neighborhoods that sat outside institutional investment for decades.

The Wall Street Journal
This New Loan Is Bringing Investors to Abandoned Towns

The post Private Lenders Fuel Investor Rush Into Distressed Rust Belt Housing appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: What Fisher Brothers Learned Building AI Into a Portfolio With Legacy Systems
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Fisher Brothers is transforming real estate with an AI lab focused on two-week sprints, legacy system integration, and scalable automation.

The post What Fisher Brothers Learned Building AI Into a Portfolio With Legacy Systems appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Fisher Brothers has been in business since 1915, started by three brothers who learned masonry from their immigrant father started building homes outside Manhattan. The firm outlasted the Depression, survived several real estate cycles, and has become one of the old guard of American real estate ownership groups. It now manages roughly $6.1 billion in assets, including about 10 million square feet of Class A office across New York, Washington, and Miami, along with 1,500 multifamily units and AREA15, the immersive entertainment district it developed off the Las Vegas Strip.

A portfolio built over that long a period carries a specific kind of technology problem. Buildings were acquired or developed in different decades, each arriving with whatever systems were standard at the time, and very little of it was designed to work together. That is the environment any AI effort at the firm has to operate in.

The push to address it came from the top and arrived quickly.

“Our CEO Winston Fisher is very forward thinking, the moment ChatGPT was released he really decided to lean into AI and that is why we made the decision to start a lab dedicated to how we could harness AI,” said Mark Stutzman, Chief Technology Officer at Fisher Brothers.

Stutzman wanted the lab to try a lot of different new ideas, which meant that he couldn’t get his team bogged down into one large project. So, he self implements a time limit that they have for each initiative. “Early on we made the decision that everything we do has to be able to be completed in a two week sprint,” Stutzman said. “This forces everyone to really focus on what can be deployed.”

Most corporate AI efforts stall somewhere between the pilot and production, usually because the scope grew during development until the thing being built no longer resembled what anyone agreed to. A two-week limit eliminates the scope creep that can come with big tech integrations. It also pushes the teams to focus on projects that can provide quick ROI.

The lab’s other function is understanding what the organization needs from automated technology, which means spending time inside the business units rather than in a technology silo. “Part of our mission is to sit with each business department and understand the tasks that could be automated with agents,” Stutzman said. Leasing, accounting, property management, and development all run processes that look automatable in the abstract and reveal their actual complexity only in conversation with the people executing them.

Deployment across the portfolio is where a company like Fisher Brothers can run into issues with legacy technology. An automation that works in one building may have nothing to connect to in another, and portfolio-wide rollouts run into whatever each property happens to be running.

AREA15 is the rare exception where a property was built around the technology, not the other way around. Fisher Brothers acquired the land in 2005 and opened the district in 2020 as a joint venture with Beneville Studios. It has drawn more than 16 million visitors since, expanded through Zone 2 in August 2025, and now anchors a larger district the City of Las Vegas has designated for development. Because it was built from scratch relatively recently, its systems share an architecture.

“Fisher Brothers properties have lots of legacy systems and unstructured data,” Stutzman said. “AREA15 was built around data so it has been very different how we have been able to roll it out.”

The lab’s longer-term work addresses the need for AI infrastructure, and Stutzman describes it in infrastructural rather than application terms. “What we are building today is the foundation of the brain,” he said. “The idea is that each app has its own MCP connectors so all of the governance and permissions are already built in.”

Model Context Protocol connectors give AI systems a standardized way to reach an application’s data and functions. Building governance and permissions into those connectors rather than into each AI tool means access rules get enforced once at the source rather than reimplemented every time something new gets deployed. For a firm with a varied application portfolio, that is the difference between integration work that compounds and integration work that repeats.

With so many possible uses of AI, prioritizing projects required a system of its own. “We use a value tracker that aggregates the benefits of each project with a score and gives the teams a way to submit their requests,” Stutzman said. “Once a month, we go through all of those and look at what we think would be the most impactful to continue to work on.”

Sourcing feedback from the people that will be using the AI also helps shed light on any areas that are possibly being overlooked.

Stutzman summaried his advice with one line of what the effort has taught him is less about technology than about sequencing. “Don’t fall into the trap of trying to boil the ocean.” Instead he advocates for short projects that can help expose where teh larger work will likely have to take place. “Take digestible chunks and think about how your overall architecture will help standardize the process,” he said. Fisher Brothers is hoping that their AI lab initiative will help them harness AI today that will help solve for the needs of tomorrow.

item.title: Rising Refinancing Costs Set to Divide Commercial Property Performance
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Wells Fargo executives say higher interest rates will compress commercial property values at refinancing, though stress has not yet materialized across the portfolio.

The post Rising Refinancing Costs Set to Divide Commercial Property Performance appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Wells Fargo executives told investors Tuesday that rising interest rates will push down commercial real estate valuations as properties refinance, though the bank sees no acute distress yet. Chief Financial Officer Mike Santomassimo said the relationship is straightforward: higher rates mean lower valuations when all other factors remain constant. CEO Charlie Scharf emphasized the bank feels confident about its own commercial real estate portfolio. Wells Fargo shares dropped 3.1% in regular trading following the earnings release.

Santomassimo said property performance will vary widely depending on whether net operating income can absorb higher debt costs during refinancing. Some buildings will handle the transition without issue, while others will face increased financial pressure. The comments come as owners confront refinancing at rates substantially higher than those locked in during the early pandemic years. Recent reporting shows that higher borrowing costs are already forcing buyers to renegotiate purchase prices or walk away from deals that no longer generate acceptable returns.

Wells Fargo’s cautious tone matches broader industry concern about a wave of maturing commercial loans facing costlier debt. Scharf noted that while the bank’s consumer lending businesses continue to grow and customer fundamentals remain solid, underwriting standards now account for an eventual weakening in credit conditions. The bank has not yet observed signs of consumer stress, but executives acknowledged that economic cycles are unavoidable. Property owners with strong cash flow will navigate refinancing more easily than those operating on thin margins or in weaker markets.

San Francisco Business Times
Wells Fargo Exec Warns Higher Interest Rates Will Hurt Commercial Real Estate Valuations. ‘It’s Just Math’

item.title: Real Estate Is About to Get Its Own Flood of AI Slop
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Authentic expertise matters more than production volume

The post Real Estate Is About to Get Its Own Flood of AI Slop appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
3 days 16 hr agoOct. 13, 2026 5:17 pm

The volume of video content real estate agents produce is about to increase by an order of magnitude. Content production has always been the constraint. Filming takes time, editing takes more, and both compete directly with the work that actually generates commissions. Ryan Serhant’s new project is the clearest signal yet that the constraint is gone. He has partnered with HeyGen to launch @HeySerhant, a channel publishing original content daily for the next twelve months through an AI avatar built on his likeness and voice. He approves the topics and signs off personally on anything tied to the market. “For an agent, every hour spent filming is an hour you’re not with a client, at a showing or working on the business,” he said, which is the entire argument in one sentence and also why this will not stay confined to one channel.

Agents are already leading into AI content production. NAR’s 2026 Realtors Technology Report found 23 percent of agents using AI daily and another 25 percent weekly, with the share using none of it falling to 21 percent from 32 percent a year earlier. Almost all of that use is content production. Seventy-five percent of AI users write listing descriptions, 56 percent write social posts, and 52 percent draft emails. Fifty-four percent named generative AI for content creation as the thing they most want to add over the next twelve months. Video has been the holdout because video required being on camera, and that requirement has now become optional.

Other industries have already found ways to harness AI content production. Graphite found that roughly half of newly published English-language articles are now primarily AI-generated, up from about ten percent before ChatGPT. Pew Research Center analyzed 490,000 pages from Common Crawl and found 10 percent of its July 2026 sample carried significant signs of AI authorship, against roughly one percent in January 2021, with more than a third of post-2022 pages showing those markers.

But just like every trend, there will be a correctio. Graphite found only about 14 percent of articles surfacing in Google Search were AI-written against 86 percent human, which suggests the ranking systems sorted the problem out well ahead of the people creating it. Google now explicitly demotes what it calls scaled content abuse. Consumer sentiment moved in the same direction. A Fractl survey of 1,008 US consumers found the share saying heavy AI use would reduce their trust in a favorite brand doubled from 20 percent in 2025 to roughly 40 percent in 2026, with only 14 percent saying it would increase trust. A June 2026 Harris Poll found 78 percent of consumers believe AI makes advertising feel less authentic and 63 percent are less likely to buy from a brand using AI-generated ads.

Real estate carries an exposure that general marketing does not, because the product being sold is a person. Agents compete on familiarity and judgment, and content exists to demonstrate both. Serhant acknowledged this directly, calling real estate a trust business and noting that HeyGen builds avatars of the actual user rather than a generic presenter. An avatar of a specific agent saying something generic about interest rates is still generic, and the likeness does not compensate for the content.

That is not an argument for abstaining. Content has been part of the playbook since the first open house flyer, and the agents who built durable businesses on Instagram and YouTube did it through years of consistency rather than individual viral moments. Consistency was always the expensive part, and it is the part this technology genuinely addresses. An agent with real expertise in a specific submarket who has never had the time to communicate it now has a way to do so.

Production cost was never what made content valuable, but it functioned as a filter. The friction of setting up a camera forced a moment of deciding whether there was anything worth recording. Removing that friction increases output but could lower the value. What becomes scarce is not production but the value of the content itself. A point of view. Specific knowledge about a specific market. Something that could not have been generated from the prompt “post about the housing market.” The ability to publish daily is about to become universal. The reason to watch will not be.

The post Real Estate Is About to Get Its Own Flood of AI Slop appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Condo Buyers Fund Construction With Bonds in Beverly Hills Tower Deal
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
A London developer is raising over $1.6 billion from condo buyers through subordinated bonds to finance its $10 billion Beverly Hills project.

The post Condo Buyers Fund Construction With Bonds in Beverly Hills Tower Deal appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Cain, a London-based investment firm, is raising capital for its $10 billion One Beverly Hills project by selling bonds to the same buyers purchasing its condos. Condo purchasers have already provided around $350 million through what Cain calls Founder Bonds, which pay a 5 percent return and are typically worth 30 percent of the purchase price. The developer aims to raise more than $1.6 billion through the program. All buyers so far have agreed to participate, though the program is voluntary.

The bonds are subordinate to a $2.8 billion senior loan led by J.P. Morgan and a $1.5 billion mezzanine loan from VICI Properties, putting buyers at risk if the project fails to complete. California law limits developer deposits to 3 percent of purchase price and bars using those funds for construction, but those restrictions do not apply to the bonds. The 5 percent return now trails the 10-year Treasury yield, which recently exceeded 5.3 percent. David Reiss, a professor at Cornell Law School, said buyers are accepting a large amount of risk for a small return, though wealthy purchasers may be better positioned to absorb potential losses.

One Beverly Hills, scheduled for completion in 2029 on 17.5 acres, will include Aman-operated condos starting at $15 million, hotel suites, high-end retail, and botanical gardens. Recent sales have exceeded $7,000 per square foot, and one penthouse reserved in July would sell for $200 million. More than $1 billion in units are under contract or reserved. Cain says it has the funds to complete the project without the bonds, but the buyer financing would replace some of its equity commitment.

Los Angeles condo sales through August were the lowest on record since 2012, according to Redfin, and several recent luxury condo projects have ended in developer defaults. Michael Shvo defaulted on a $200 million loan at the Beverly Hills Mandarin Oriental in 2024 and sold remaining units in bulk the following year. Brokers say the ultraluxury market above $10 million attracts different buyers seeking lock-and-leave flexibility, and Beverly Hills has continued to perform even as other parts of the city have declined.

The Wall Street Journal
The Luxury Beverly Hills Condo Project Borrowing Money From Its Future Residents
